title: Simple Network Time Protocol (SNTP) Version 4 for IPv4, IPv6 and OSI
summary: SNTPv4 is a simplified subset of the Network Time Protocol for devices that need to set their clocks over the network but do not need the full precision of NTP. It clarifies header formats and a simple, stateless request-and-response mode for IPv4, IPv6, and OSI. It also gives guidance to makers of home and business devices on avoiding abuse of time servers. It obsoleted RFC 1769 and RFC 2030, and was itself replaced by RFC 5905.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of wearing a perfect watch that you keep adjusting, you just ask a friend what time it is and set your watch from the answer. Simple gadgets do that with a time server.

subtitle: A lightweight protocol for devices to synchronize their clocks over the network.

tldr.problem: Devices need to keep their clocks accurate, but a full Network Time Protocol implementation is too complex for simple gadgets like home routers.
tldr.mechanism: SNTP is a simplified subset of NTP that uses a lightweight request-response exchange: a client asks a time server for the current time and uses the answer to set its clock. It adds minimal overhead with an 8-byte header and requires no persistent state at the server.
tldr.outcome: SNTP is no longer recommended: RFC 5905 superseded it with a more comprehensive time synchronization specification. However, it remains in use in many simple devices.

sections.title: Simple Synchronization
sections.content:
SNTP is a lightweight protocol that lets devices synchronize their clocks with a network time server. Unlike the full Network Time Protocol (NTP), which provides high precision and complex algorithms for managing distributed time sources, SNTP is designed for devices that need simpler, less accurate time synchronization: accuracy on the order of fractions of a second to a minute is acceptable, such as in home routers and simple appliances.

The protocol uses the same message format as NTP but operates in a simple, stateless request-response mode. A client sends a request to a server, the server responds with the current time, and the client uses that response to update its clock. No persistent state or complex algorithms are required at the server.
sections.plainLanguage: You send a message asking 'What time is it?' and the server replies with the current time. You set your clock and you are done.

sections.title: The SNTP Message Format
sections.content:
Every SNTP message begins with an 8-byte header followed by optional data. The header contains four 16-bit fields: source port, destination port, length, and checksum. The source port is optional and can be set to zero if not used; the destination port identifies the receiving application. The length field counts the header and data in bytes, so its minimum value is eight. The checksum covers a pseudo-header taken from the IP layer, the SNTP header, and the data, providing basic error detection.

The message includes four 64-bit timestamp fields: the reference timestamp (when the server last updated its clock), the originate timestamp (when the client sent the request), the receive timestamp (when the server received the request), and the transmit timestamp (when the server sent the reply). These four timestamps allow the client to calculate the round-trip delay and the clock offset relative to the server.

SNTP uses the same timestamp format as NTP: a 64-bit unsigned value representing seconds since 0h on 1 January 1900, with 32 bits for the integer part and 32 bits for the fractional part. This format allows for multiple-precision arithmetic and convenient conversion to other time representations.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is the address label on the postcard: who sent it, who it is for, how big it is, and a check number to spot if it got scrambled. The four timestamps are 'when was this clock last set' and three times that record the journey of the message back and forth.

sections.title: Operating Modes
sections.content:
SNTP supports three operating modes: unicast, broadcast, and manycast. In unicast mode, a client sends a request to a designated server and expects a reply. This mode requires the client to know the server's address beforehand. In broadcast mode, a server periodically sends unsolicited messages to a broadcast address; clients listen on that address and extract the time. Broadcast mode is efficient for many clients but requires them to be on the same network segment and provides less accuracy than unicast because clients cannot measure round-trip delay.

Manycast mode is a hybrid: the client sends a request to a broadcast address where multiple servers listen. Any server that hears the request can reply directly to the client. The client binds to the server from which it receives the first reply and continues operation in unicast mode. This allows clients to discover time servers without prior configuration.

The protocol uses UDP port 123 (assigned by IANA to NTP/SNTP). SNTP operates over IPv4, IPv6, and OSI networks. The same message format works for all three, though the handling of reference identifiers differs when dealing with IPv6 and OSI addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The client can ask one specific server for the time, listen to broadcasts from any server on the network, or send a call to whoever is listening and use the first to reply. All of these modes send the same kinds of messages.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
An SNTP client initializes the message header with specific values: the mode field is set to 3 (client), the version number is set to the highest version supported (typically 4), and the transmit timestamp is set to the client's current time. All other fields are zero. When the server reply arrives, the client extracts the transmit timestamp and uses the four timestamps to calculate the round-trip delay and clock offset using simple arithmetic formulas, then updates its system clock.

An SNTP server is stateless: it does not store information about clients. When it receives a request, it copies the client's transmit timestamp to the originate field of the reply, records the time the request arrived (receive timestamp), and records the time it sends the reply (transmit timestamp). If the server is synchronized to an external time source (such as a GPS receiver or radio clock), it sets the stratum field to 1 and includes a reference identifier indicating the source. If unsynchronized, it sets the stratum to 0 and can include a 'kiss-o'-death' message to tell clients to go elsewhere.

Servers normally operate at stratum 1 (primary server) with a dedicated external time source and should not operate at higher strata. Broadcast servers should also respond to unicast requests so potential broadcast clients can measure propagation delay before switching to listen-only broadcast mode.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a request with the time it thinks it is, and the server sends back its time along with the arrival and departure times. The client uses these four time points to figure out how long the message took to travel and adjust its clock accordingly.

sections.title: Network Best Practices
sections.content:
SNTP deployment increased dramatically as millions of devices (routers, Windows PCs, Cisco equipment, embedded systems) gained network time support. However, poorly configured SNTP clients can consume significant server and network resources. The RFC establishes guidelines for device manufacturers and developers: clients must not send requests more frequently than every 15 seconds, should increase the time between requests (poll interval) as the clock synchronizes, should use local servers when available to avoid backbone traffic, and must allow operators to configure the primary and backup servers.

Most importantly, clients must support the 'kiss-o'-death' mechanism: when a server sends a reply with stratum 0, the client must stop sending requests to that server and switch to a backup. The kiss codes (such as DENY for access denied or RATE for rate limit exceeded) communicate why the server is declining service. This mechanism prevents the cascading failures that occurred when misconfigured home routers sent requests at one-second intervals to overloaded public time servers.
sections.plainLanguage: If many devices all ask the same time server for the time too often, the server gets overwhelmed. Good devices ask less often, ask nearby servers first, and stop asking a server if it tells them to go away.

fields.name: LI/VN/Mode
fields.desc: Leap indicator (2 bits), version (3 bits), mode (3 bits).

fields.name: Stratum
fields.desc: Clock stratum: 1 for primary server, 2-15 for secondary, 0 for kiss-o'-death.

fields.name: Poll Interval
fields.desc: Exponent of 2 for maximum interval between messages, in seconds.

fields.name: Precision
fields.desc: Signed exponent of 2 for system clock precision, in seconds.

fields.name: Root Delay
fields.desc: Round-trip delay from client to primary server, in seconds.

fields.name: Root Dispersion
fields.desc: Maximum clock frequency error, in seconds.

fields.name: Reference Identifier
fields.desc: Clock source identifier (ASCII) or IPv4 address of sync source.

fields.name: Reference Timestamp
fields.desc: Time when system clock was last updated.

fields.name: Receive Timestamp
fields.desc: Time when request arrived at server.
